title_zh: 第二十一類 僧道騙

stories.title_en: A Monk Claims a Cow Is His Mother

paragraphs.en: In the sixth month of summer, a traveling monk was passing along the road when he saw a herd-boy tending a herd of cattle. Among them was a large, fat yellow cow. The herd-boy held out his left foot for the cow to lick, and she licked it; then he offered his right foot, and she licked that too. The monk asked, "Why does this cow lick your feet?" The boy replied, "This cow is very tame, and I am very fond of her. My feet sweat a lot and taste salty, so she loves to lick them." Realizing that the cow was fond of salt, the monk quietly noted her down and learned that she belonged to the household of Elder Suo.

The next day the monk took thick salt brine and smeared it generously over his head, face, and entire body, hands, and feet. He went to Elder Suo's house, knelt at the gate weeping, and said: "Please show compassion and deliver my mother and me." Elder Suo replied, "I cannot preach or recite sutras; how could I deliver anyone?" The monk said, "While my late mother was alive, she refused to keep vegetarian fasts or give alms. Now that she has been dead for seven years, I know she must be suffering punishment in the underworld. However, our family is poor, and I cannot afford the rites to save her. Admiring Mulian's rescue of his mother, I shaved my head and became a monk, seeking only to deliver her. Last month I met a wise teacher who told me my old mother had been reborn as a yellow cow in your household. I have come respectfully to ask that she be delivered." Elder Suo said, "I have four cows in the pen. How would one know which one it is?" The monk replied, "Please let me go with you to look. Beasts possess even more spiritual nature. When mother and child meet, there will surely be affection, unlike the others." Elder Suo went with the monk to the pen and released the cattle. When the monk saw the large cow approach, he removed his cap, knelt forward weeping, and said, "This is my mother!" The cow smelled the salt and licked his head and face all over, appearing full of pity. The monk wept even more, then taken off his clothes; the cow licked his entire body and would not leave. Elder Suo saw that it was truly strange—just like a mother's love for her child, except it could not speak. He asked, "If this is your mother from a former life, what must be done now to deliver her?" The monk said, "If I had silver, I would buy her at half price and raise her, but this poor monk's robe and bowl are empty. I beg the elder to grant her to me temporarily. I will lead her to a mountain hermitage, gather grass daily, and cook gruel to feed her. When her punishment is complete and her natural lifespan ends, I will bury her and recite sutras to deliver her, so that in the next life she may be reborn as a human and not fall into the animal path." The elder, moved by the earnestness of his words, said, "I grant her to you." The monk kowtowed in thanks, led the cow three days' journey away, and left her at a hermitage to be cared for.

When the tenth month came and the weather turned cold, the monk called a butcher to slaughter the cow, giving half the meat to the butcher, who sold it for one tael and five qian of silver; the other half the monk kept for himself, curing and drying it into provisions that he hid throughout the lining of his patched robe. Then he went straight to Elder Suo's hall and sat down cross-legged in full lotus. The elder came out and asked, "What monk dares come up into my hall and sit?" The monk said, "Do you happen to recognize me?" The elder said, "I do not know who you are—how would I recognize you?" The monk said, "Doesn't my face look naturally familiar to you?" The elder said, "We have never met; where would any familiarity come from?" The monk heaved a long sigh: "Your original spiritual nature has been completely lost—no wonder you fail to recognize an old friend's features!" The elder asked, "What do you mean, an old friend?" The monk said, "In the past, Master Foyin awakened Su Dongpo, and Master Huiyuan called back Bai Letian—were they not old friends of Su and Bai from former lives? In your previous life you cultivated the Way alongside me, but because your worldly desires were not yet severed, you were reborn here to enjoy this earthly wealth. I have come expressly to deliver you. You should quickly cast aside your worldly debts and return to diligent cultivation, so as not to waste the merit of your former life." The elder asked, "How can you know of former lives?" The monk replied, "My cultivation is twice yours. While you have been enjoying half a lifetime of worldly fortune, I have added half a lifetime of bitter ascetic practice—why would it be hard for me to know the karmic causes of three lifetimes?" The elder asked, "What bitter practice have you undertaken in this life?" The monk said, "Never mind my earlier austerities—for the past three years I have abstained completely from grain." Startled at last, the elder said, "If you can abstain from grain, what say you fast for one month here in my house?" The monk laughed: "After three years of it, what is a single month?" The elder asked, "Do you still take tea or hot water?" The monk replied, "Only a single bowl of clear tea or boiling water a day." So the elder kept him there, had an empty room swept clean for him to sit in, and sent in one bowl of tea in the morning and one bowl of boiling water at night.

He sat there for seven days, then was invited out again and answered just as before. The elder was amazed and convinced, asking, "How should I cultivate?" The monk replied, "Just abandon your household and go far away; the proper way to practice will present itself." The elder said, "My wife would be left a widow and my children are young. Who would inherit the property? This I cannot do. What is the next-best cultivation?" The monk said, "Only giving. Repair temples and serve the Buddha, and in the next life you will receive blessed rewards. Right now, a hermitage on Mount Lu is being rebuilt by a single donor. If you donate five hundred taels to complete the repair at once, that too is a great merit." The elder followed his advice, sent a servant with the monk to deliver five hundred taels, handed them over clearly to the abbot, kept the servant for several days, then sent him back to report to his master. Later, the monk took two hundred fifty taels from the donation and departed. As for moving the rich man with fasting from grain, he was privately eating the dried provisions he had brought. Who would believe anyone truly fasts from grain!

Note: This monk making off with the cow was still the lesser offense; he could have resold her. To call her his mother from a past life and then slaughter and eat her—the crime towers over Heaven. Then using her as dried provisions while falsely claiming to fast from grain: that swindle too was great. Though half the offering went to the monastery, it was still a good deed, and the monk would gain the merit of soliciting donations. But relieving urgent needs and aiding the poor should be directed to neighbors; why must it be thrown into a monastery? This is the fault of fools who believe in the profits of the field of merit—and of not having read Master Fu Yi's Gaoshi zhuan.

stories.title_en: Taking Infant Elixir to Fake Fasting from Grain

paragraphs.en: There was a monk who claimed he could live without grain. Rich families often summoned him to test it. For seven or eight days running he would not eat a single grain, or every two or three days he would take only one bowl of boiling water. His name spread widely, and people competed to give him gold and silk. A local official, seeing Magistrate Chu, happened to mention this, saying the world had such an eminent monk, truly an immortal or Buddha born again. Master Chu was most upright, and had never believed monks and Daoists. He said: "People receive this physical body. How can they cut off food and sex? Those who pretend to live without grain only hide dried provisions in secret, to fool the ignorant. How can a gentleman who understands principle believe this sort? If they could truly live without grain, they would flee far into the deep mountains, fearing only that their fame would reach the world. Why would they wander the markets? And if they accept gifts of gold and silk, what would they use them for?" The local official, rebuked by Master Chu, felt as if he himself had been caught believing swindlers, and wanted still more to prove his words were true. So he said: "If Your Honor does not believe, you may summon him and test him, and then you will know this junior's words are not false."

Master Chu immediately had men summon him and ordered his body searched. Nothing else was hidden on him, only twenty-four Amitabha beads, which he was permitted to keep. They swept out a clean room, spread a bed and mat for him to sit upon, and stationed people outside to watch him in secret rotation. Each day, someone would open the door openly to take a look, then lock it again upon leaving. For two days, he sat in full lotus posture, his appearance unchanged. On the third day, when they opened the door to look, they saw sweat of exhaustion on his face, and he asked for boiling water to drink. Master Chu ordered it given, and after they left and locked the door, the secret watchers reported: "The monk mixed one Amitabha bead into the water, drank it, and his countenance recovered." Thereafter, every two days they sent in a bowl of boiling water, and the watchers always reported: "He mixed in a bead and swallowed it."

After eleven days, Master Chu summoned the monk out, took his Amitabha prayer beads, and inspected them: only nineteen beads remained in his hands. Master Chu confiscated the beads, ordered the monk placed in light detention where no one was to disturb him, and left him to sit quietly awaiting judgment. He then secretly instructed the jailer: "Do not allow any monks or Daoists to come in and see him. After two days he will surely beg you for food. When he does, ask him how those Amitabha beads are made. If you can make some that, when mixed with water, turn out just like these beads, I will reward you handsomely afterward."

The next day, the monk asked the jailer for food. The jailer said, "Teach me how to make the elixir beads, and I will feed you." The monk replied, "This medicine is extremely rare. Just give me food now; when I am released, I will reward you with much silver. There is no need to ask for the formula." The jailer refused him food. After three days, the monk collapsed from starvation, his face turning green and yellow, devoid of any human color.

Master Chu had him brought out for questioning: "I knew from the start these beads were infant elixir. Confess the method of manufacture, and I will spare your life." The monk pretended to be dying and dared not answer. Master Chu laughed: "Look at this fasting monk! In front of me, he has gone three days without food and is about to starve. This elixir comes from a child in a woman's womb; you must plot to kill a pregnant woman and cut out the infant to make it. Who knows how many lives you have destroyed to create this evil karma? How dare you speak the formula aloud? Do I want your recipe? If I beat you to death, the crime would still be light." He ordered a platform built before the yamen, produced the nineteen beads, and mixed four for the common people to see. Mixed with boiling water, the whole bowl turned into a thick paste. Those who dared to drink found it fragrant and sweet; two mouthfuls were enough to last a day. The remaining fifteen were given to doctors to treat injuries and deficiencies. Then they bound the monk on the platform and executed him by lingchi (death by a thousand cuts). Master Chu said, "A county magistrate is the father and mother of the people; how could he bear to kill? But this is to vent the hatred of the many wronged." All cried out in satisfaction, and afterward the local gentry never again trusted monks or Daoists.

Note: Those who fake fasting from grain mostly hide dried provisions; those who take infant elixir are few. This food is not hidden on the body, for fear people will search. It is all entrusted to beggars; when someone tests them, they secretly pass the dried provisions to them. There are also those who take pine needles and bamboo leaves: pine needles eaten together with yangti herb, bamboo leaves eaten together with tender ferns, all slippery and edible. Monks have also used this to fool people, saying they can live on these. But from ancient times, the methods of living without grain that exist are immortal recipes, not things of the human world. I once heard of a man who met an extraordinary person who taught him to live without grain; I record it below.

On Mount Wuyi, a poor man built a hut in a bend of the cliffs, barely enough space for a bed and a stove. He cleared the mountain to plant tea, selling it to support himself. After ten-odd years, the tea slopes he had opened yielded three or four taels annually. Every day he labored without rest; only in severe cold, extreme heat, or wind and rain would he sit silent all day beneath his cliff hut. He knew no scriptures and had no dealings with others.

Suddenly one day a Daoist passed his hut and said, "You toil on the mountain. Why not hand over the tea slopes to someone else to till, receive one tael a year to buy clothes, and let me teach you a method of living without grain? Then you need not buy rice or labor on the mountain; you can sit at ease and be self-sufficient." The mountain man said, "I have heard that practitioners possess methods of living without grain. If you are willing to teach me, I will bow to you as master and ask to learn." The Daoist said, "Your nature is quiet; you are well-suited for cultivation. From now on, each morning boil two jars of clear spring water until reduced by half, then combine them into one jar and boil again. Drink two bowls each time—morning, noon, and evening. After drinking, still your mind and cease your thoughts, press your tongue to the upper palate, close your mouth and eyes, and sit quietly all day. Or if the sky is clear and your spirit fresh, go out walking: stroll slowly and look about leisurely, going wherever suits you, whether for half a day or just a moment. In walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, simply follow your mind and do not resist it. If you encounter mountain fruits or plant seeds that are edible, eating one or two causes no harm, but do not seek them intentionally. In this way you can live without grain. Remember this and do not lightly pass it to others." The mountain man followed this practice. After one year he indeed ate not a single grain of millet; his face was golden-yellow, and he was light and vigorous as ever. Neighbors living nearby often did not see him buying rice; or if they passed his hut, there was no pot or steamer visible. When asked, he answered, "In recent years I have learned a method of living without grain." The neighbors spread the wonder from one to another. Those who bowed and begged for the method would always flee and refuse to teach, saying, "My teacher ordered me not to leak it lightly." The next year the news spread near and far, and many came with letters of introduction to pay respects. Some brought grain and lodged in his hut to watch for a full month: they indeed saw him only drink boiling water, then sit quietly afterward, silent, doing nothing, with no idle talk. Those who did not understand might question him hard or discuss cultivation with him; he would smile, rise, walk the mountain paths, returning at noon or evening, then warm boiling water and drink again. He neither welcomed those who came nor saw off those who left; he did not ask people a single word. If people asked him and he could answer, he would reply with one or two sentences offhand. If they asked about other idle matters, he would shake his head and say nothing, appearing annoyed, and simply go sit quietly himself. All his speech, movement, and social responses were met with an empty mind. By the second year, his fame grew even greater. Rich households and nobles often prepared saddles and sedan chairs to receive him; he firmly fled and would not go. When the rich and noble went in person to urge and pressure him, he later visited various houses. Wherever he arrived, he would not eat a single thing from them, only sit quietly in an empty room like a wooden Buddha, except that he still spoke and moved a little.

After two and a half years, a wealthy man from Tanyang welcomed him with great ceremony, treating him even more solemnly, as if he were a deity. He would occasionally serve tea and fruit, and the man ate only a little. Later, the host prepared clear tea and fine rice, earnestly pressing him to eat. The man firmly refused, claiming he could not; yet, under pressure, he was compelled to eat one bowl. Shortly after, he grew extremely hungry and drank boiling water. Hungry again and unable to endure it, he asked for food once more. The rich man was delighted and served him respectfully. For three consecutive days, he ate five times a day, barely managing to quell his hunger. The mountain man began to suspect and fear himself, urgently requesting to return to the mountain. He resumed drinking water and sitting quietly as before, but could not escape the gnawing hunger. Eventually, he had no choice but to eat again, taking three meals like an ordinary person.

Note: The Daoist whom the mountain man met was clearly an immortal. Had he completed three years of fasting, he would surely have attained deliverance. Alas, he was burdened by fame, which drew people to welcome and serve him, forced him to eat, and caused him to ruin his prior achievements himself. This was the folly of urging him to eat. That rich man's intent was to serve him devoutly, hoping to share in the blessings of a living Buddha—was that truly a sincere heart devoted to the Way? The mountain man had already been misled, and where then were those blessings? He will also incur the sin of a hundred kalpas, and in his next life he is bound to become great enemies with the mountain man. From this we see that fasting is an immortal method, not merely a matter of drinking hot water and sitting still. Otherwise, if afterward he continued to drink and sit as before, why would he not still be able to fast? Thus, those today who feign fasting to demand money and rice are nothing but thief-monks and rogue Daoists. Would anyone truly practicing fasting dare let others know?

stories.title_en: Believing a Monk's Talk, He Nearly Came to Ruin

paragraphs.en: Ding Da of Huizhou was a charitable man who loved doing good and giving alms. One day he traveled with his friend Lin Ze to Haicheng to buy pepper and sappanwood timber, which they took to Linqing and other markets to sell; before long, all the goods were sold off. In that town stood a monastery housing a famous monk styled Wuer, just past thirty, handsome and refined in bearing, skilled at lecturing on the sutras and discoursing on karmic cause and effect. He drew countless young men from respectable families to visit the temple and pay homage, and many were moved by his preaching to shave their heads and become monks. At that time Ding Da invited Lin Ze to call on Wuer. Lin Ze warned him, "You have always been fond of charity, and I hear this monk has a clever tongue and persuasive words, repeatedly luring men into shaving their heads to become monks. If you go see him and fall under his spell, how will you return home and face your parents?" Ding Da replied, "Persuasion lies with him, but the choice rests with me. I have a mind of my own—what hold could he possibly have over me?" Insisting on going to pay his respects, he found Wuer's manner calm and graceful. Once the conversation turned to karmic cause and effect, Ding Da was deeply moved: he donated all his trading capital, entered the monastery, bowed to Wuer as his master, and resolved to shave his head and become a monk. Lin Ze grew angry: "Before we even came here, I warned you of this! Now you have truly been bewitched by his lies—how can you call yourself a man?" He pleaded earnestly with him again and again, but Ding Da refused to listen. Lin Ze returned home alone, while Ding Da remained at the temple to practice monastic cultivation.

After two years, the monk Wuer encountered Widow Dong, who came to the temple to burn incense. She was very beautiful, virtuous, and fond of reciting Amitabha. She brought along a seventeen-year-old maid, of peerless beauty and charm, who also paid respects at the temple. Wuer used clever words to persuade and lure her; the widow's heart submitted, and she immediately bowed to Wuer as her teacher, wishing to shave her head and become a nun, staying a few nights in the temple for the time being. Her maid frequently visited Wuer's room to deliver fruit and snacks. Unable to restrain his desire, Wuer offered ten taels of silver to seduce her. The maid accepted the silver and became intimate with him. Wuer then turned his thoughts to the widow. One night, he slipped into her room, waited until Mistress Dong was fast asleep, and attempted to rape her. Mistress Dong, chaste and firm, refused. She cried out, "Who is this lawless man, daring to come and rape and steal?" Before she could utter a few words, Wuer tightened a handkerchief around her neck, and within moments, she was dead.

The next day, the maid went to report to Li Ying, son of Mistress Dong. By the time they arrived at the temple, Wuer had already fled. However, Wuer had long been notorious, and people everywhere were familiar with him. Li Ying hired men to hunt him down across the region; within two days, they caught him and delivered him to the county authorities. The official immediately mustered over a hundred militia members to surround the temple. At that point, the temple monks had scattered in all directions to save their lives, leaving no one to arrest. The official then ordered the temple burned, had Wuer beaten forty strokes, and sentenced him according to the standard legal code.

Da had lost both his capital and his reputation, feeling too ashamed to return home. Later, his family learned he had fled back and sent people to find him and bring him home; only after his hair had grown long did he dare venture out. This serves as a stark lesson for fools who trust monks.

Note: Temple gates conceal villains; monks are thieves. This is common, and such cases often come to light. Even if people have not seen it with their own eyes, they have surely heard of it. Why do they still fail to take warning? Women entering temples and men becoming monks—this is truly great folly. Dong, though she died, was fortunate to preserve her chastity intact; Ding Da, though fortunate to escape with his life, had already lost his capital. If at that time he had been arrested alongside Wuer, how could they have distinguished the innocent from the guilty? He would surely have died in prison with him. Therefore, those who use heretical talk to lure others—whether scholars, farmers, artisans, or merchants—should all refuse to believe them and keep their distance.

stories.title_en: A Monk Resembling the Temple Guardian Fakes a Fundraising Appeal

paragraphs.en: Tianyuan Temple had been dilapidated for years. The abbot Wanlang intended to repair it, but feared the labor and cost would be enormous; unless a wealthy benefactor vowed to undertake it single-handedly, it would be hard to get started. One day, a wandering monk named Ruobing came to lodge at the temple. He was tall and sturdy, with a square black face, round eyes, and long ears—exactly like the image of the temple's guardian deity. Wanlang was delighted at the sight, prepared a vegetarian feast that night to receive him, and treated him with extra diligence and respect. The next day, Monk Ruobing said, "This precious monastery is not flourishing. Why then are you so willing to welcome monks from all quarters?" Wanlang replied, "The one who will revive my temple depends on your esteemed help. I dare greatly to rely on you." Ruobing said, "Our mountain household has thin karmic ties. How can I possibly help?" Wanlang said, "This temple needs five hundred taels to be fully repaired. Even collecting small amounts from many donors won't suffice. Looking at your honored appearance, you resemble our temple's guardian perfectly. I ask you to seek out a hugely rich family. If you solicit funds from them for the full repair, wait until they are wavering between yes and no, arrange for them to come to the temple to see it in person, and I will have my own method to secure them."

Ruobing understood. He went to the edge of the great river, where a timber merchant named Jing Xiuyun held capital worth tens of thousands. Ruobing carried dried provisions, entered the timber raft yard, loudly chanted a sutra, sat in lotus position, and called out, "Collecting alms!" The merchant ordered his men to give him money. The monk ignored it entirely, saying, "I am not collecting paltry cash. This poor monk shares a karmic bond with the donor and seeks a thousand taels." Xiuyun frowned: "What use is collecting a thousand taels?" The monk replied, "Two hundred li from here lies Tianyuan Temple. When it was first founded, you had a karmic connection there, which is why you are so wealthy in this life. Recently, it has fallen into ruin. It needs five hundred taels for repairs and another five hundred for an endowment to support incense and lamps; thereafter, it will endure, and your merit will be vast." Xiuyun asked, "You are collecting donations for the temple. What karmic connection did you have with it in a past life?" The monk said, "The temple is my place of residence and sustenance. Without a karmic bond, how could I dwell there long?" Xiuyun ignored him. The monk remained on the timber raft for three days without leaving. If the men gave him rice, he ate; if they did not, he also did not eat. After four more days, Xiuyun said, "I will give three hundred taels to help. Go collect from others instead." The monk replied, "If I cannot collect from one with a karmic bond, why waste words on those without?" Xiuyun said, "Bring the donation ledger. I will write down three hundred taels." The monk said, "The ledger is at the temple. Three hundred is insufficient anyway; no need to write it. If you seek only blessings in this life, give five hundred taels. If you wish to pave the way for the next life, nothing less than a thousand taels will suffice." Xiuyun said, "I do not believe in this life or the next. Take these three hundred taels and go; kindly proceed with the repairs. If it is not enough, surely other good people will help?" The monk said, "Why would I want the silver? You send it directly to the abbot." Xiuyun said, "I will deliver it to the temple in ten days." The monk then joined his palms, recited "Amitabha Buddha" once, and departed. He returned and recounted the matter in detail to Wanlang, adding, "In ten days the timber merchant will come; I shall stay far away." Wanlang was greatly pleased and early prepared tea, fruit, and vegetarian dishes to await them.

On the tenth day, Xiuyun indeed arrived with the silver and two servants. Knowing he was the timber merchant, Abbot Wanlang received him with solemn courtesy, served tea, and asked, "What is the benefactor's honored surname?" Xiuyun replied, "Jing." Wanlang asked, "Where has the benefactor come from?" Xiuyun said, "Earlier I made an appointment with a fundraising monk from this precious monastery, so today I have respectfully come up from the river." Wanlang pondered a moment and said, "Our mountain temple has not sent anyone out to solicit donations." Xiuyun said, "Seventeen days ago, a monk sat in meditation in my timber loft for seven days, and I promised him I would come today." Wanlang said, "None of the monks of this temple have gone out during the past half month; it must have been a wandering monk falsely using our name." He at once ordered a vegetarian meal prepared to entertain him. Inwardly, Xiuyun found it strange: "If it was a wandering monk falsely using their name, why didn't he take the silver that day?" Keeping the doubt to himself, he strolled around the temple grounds. When he entered the shrine of the Temple Guardian, he looked up and saw that the statue of the guardian looked just like the monk from the other day. His two servants also pointed and said, "This Temple Guardian looks the very image of that monk!" More amazed than ever, Xiuyun suspected in his heart that the Temple Guardian himself had manifested as a monk to urge him to repair the monastery. He bowed and prayed: "If the monk of the other day was your manifestation, grant me a holy cast of the divination blocks." He cast the blocks at once and got a holy sign. He prayed again: "I have brought three hundred taels today; I pray for great profit this year." Casting again, he got a yang sign. He said, "If three hundred taels is not enough and you want five hundred, grant me a holy cast." This time he got a yin sign. He prayed once more: "Now I understand in my heart. If you want an additional five hundred taels for incense-and-lamp fields, grant me a holy cast." Sure enough, he threw a holy sign. Having bowed in thanks, Xiuyun returned to the vegetarian feast and asked Wanlang, "How much silver is needed for the repairs?" Wanlang replied, "I have long wished to repair the temple. The other day I had craftsmen estimate the cost, and they said it would take five hundred taels in all, so I dared not begin." Xiuyun said, "The other day I promised three hundred taels, which I have brought with me now, and tomorrow I will send two hundred more to make up the sum. Once the repairs are complete, I will donate another five hundred taels to purchase incense-and-lamp fields to serve the Buddha forever." Overjoyed at these words, Wanlang pressed his palms together and bowed down. Later, after Xiuyun had donated the full amount as promised, the wandering monk Ruobing secretly took two hundred taels as his share and departed.

Note: The monk's appearance resembled that of the temple guardian, so this trick was cleverly pieced together; one might even call it remarkable. Yet, these people concocted this scheme—where did they truly become incarnations of the guardian? Thus, being wealthy and generous is inherently a virtuous act. If one claims that a true Buddha collecting alms guarantees blessings for those who donate, could these two fraudulent monks bestow such blessings upon anyone? I do not believe it.

stories.title_en: Faking Foresight to Cheat a Man Out of a Silk Robe

paragraphs.en: Jiang Dajian of Dongyang inherited ten thousand taels from his father. However, because the prefectural treasury clerks had repeatedly infiltrated and exploited him, more than half his family fortune was squandered. He also had a fondness for male favorites, keeping handsome young servants to attend him wherever he went. One day, Liang, a friend of Jiang's, met one of these servants and asked, "The other day, two bolts of dark silk bought for your master were both extra long. Surely there must be leftovers after making a long robe?" The servant replied, "The tailor was incompetent. The first robe he made was too long to wear; the second one was just right." Liang said, "Why not cut the long one shorter? What harm is there?" The servant said, "He doesn't want it anyway; it's already been put away in the large chest in the study." In fact, Jiang owned many garments; any he no longer wore after using them were tossed into that chest. Liang said, "How can one bear to discard a new garment? Tell him to give it to me so I can alter it to fit." The servant said, "If you wish to ask him for it, the third item in the chest is that new robe."

A monk nearby overheard this. Knowing Jiang Dajian was generous, he pretended to be a wandering monk and entered Master Jiang's yamen quarters to solicit donations. Jiang gave him two cash. The monk said, "I see an air of grievance throughout the entire yamen, yet only in your residence does auspicious light fill the rooms. You will surely secure a good official post with a bright future ahead. Let me beg for a fine robe from you to establish a karmic bond." Jiang replied, "I have no fine robes." The monk said, "You have one you cannot wear. Give it to me; that would be excellent." Jiang feigned ignorance, saying, "All my clothes can be worn. How could there be one I cannot wear?" The monk insisted, "It is a new dark-silk robe, too long, kept in the large chest in the study. The third item should be given to me. I will dispel your disasters and extend your life. Otherwise, immediate calamity awaits you." Jiang found this strange, opened the chest, and indeed found two items on top, with the new silk robe as the third. Suspecting the monk had foresight, he took it out and gave it to him, asking, "Having given this robe, can I be spared the trouble?" The monk replied, "I was merely testing whether you possess a kind heart. Since you are now willing to give, disaster has already turned into fortune."

Note: Monks today are all ordinary men. How can they know the future? When they speak of past events, they mostly get them from hearsay; when they speak of future events, they are all false claims. Looking at how this monk cheated Master Jiang, those today who call themselves spiritual guides are all of this type. Master Jiang was so easy to cheat—how could the household not fail? Those in the world who believe monks' lures may take this as a warning.
